1.pericope_label: Rachel’s envy, and the sons of the two handmaids

schools.summary: Gill takes Rachel's wrestlings for importunate prayer while noting a rival rendering that makes them craftiness, and hears in the name of Leah's maid's first son either a troop of children or the commander of a troop who should head an army, agreeing with Jacob's later prophecy. Calvin blames Rachel for seeking a triumph by unlawful arts instead of fleeing to God, and blames Jacob for departing from a divine command to please a wife who stood in no such place; yet he grants that God honoured the connection with offspring, that its children were reckoned legitimate, and that a union void from the beginning obtained by special privilege the honour of wedlock. He thinks Leah the greater sinner for despairing after a short pause when she had already known the blessing, canvasses joining and doubling for the second name before settling on wrestlings called divine because Hebrew marks excellence by adding God's name, rejects outright the notion that Gad names a planet, and makes Leah boast instead of the number of her children.

Henry traces the whole trouble to the marriage with two sisters, contrasting Rachel with the long-childless Rebekah, over whom no such quarrel arose. He finds three faults in Rachel's demand — that one child would not content her, that her heart was set on it inordinately, and that she asked her husband rather than God — and sets her beside Hannah, who wept where Rachel envied and was submissive where Rachel was peremptory. Jacob's rebuke he holds just and loving, a reproof needing to be warm like a medicine, neither so hot as to scald nor so cold as to be useless; he collects the Chaldee and Arabic paraphrases of Jacob's question, and repeats the rabbinic saying that the keys of the clouds, the heart, the grave and the womb are entrusted to no angel. Of the rivalry between the sisters he observes only that it shows the wisdom of an appointment joining one man to one woman.

Clarke explains the standing of the handmaid, whose person and children alike were the mistress's property, so that she bore vicariously, which is the force of bearing upon the knees, and glosses Rachel's phrase as being built up, since the word for son derives from the word for building and a family is composed of children as a house of stones. On the second name he prefers a root meaning to twist and quotes Parkhurst for the sense that Rachel's family is now entwined with her sister's and may yet produce the promised Seed, while admitting the original is hard to fix; on the third he reports the renderings troop, army, soldier and planet, thinks Laban's judicial astrology makes a reference to Jupiter possible, and adds the Greek, Latin and an old English version that gave it as an exclamation of good luck. Wesley follows Henry on the rivalry of the sisters and the names given as trophies.

Ellicott explains that the newborn was laid first on the father's knees, whose acceptance acknowledged the child, and then on the mother's, and holds Rachel less excusable than Sarah, since no religious hope was involved but only vexation and envy, allowing in her defence only that the custom existed and may have been counted meritorious because distasteful to the wife. He observes that Leah speaks of Jehovah where Rachel speaks of Elohim, attributing this partly to Rachel's half-idolatry and noting that she uses the covenant name once she bears a child of her own; and he defends the received rendering of the second name, denying that wrestling here means prayer since the passage usually cited employs a different verb, and calling the victory discreditable, won by a bad custom and consisting in weaning Jacob further from the unloved Leah. Keil and Delitzsch sum the sequence up as two wives carried away by constant jealousy over their husband's attachment.

debates: What the second son's name means. Gill takes it for wrestlings of prayer but records a rendering that makes it craftiness; Clarke prefers a root meaning to twist and follows Parkhurst in reading the families as entwined; Ellicott upholds the common rendering and rejects the prayer sense on the ground that the passage cited uses another verb; Calvin weighs joining and doubling before settling on wrestlings called divine by a Hebrew idiom of excellence.

What the name Gad refers to. Clarke allows that it may name a planet, given Laban's dealings in judicial astrology, and reports renderings from good fortune to good luck; Calvin denies that Leah would extol a planet instead of God and, guided by Jacob's later blessing, refers the name to the abundance of her children; Gill takes it of a troop, whether of children or of soldiers under a commander.

How far Rachel and Jacob are excusable. Ellicott allows Rachel less excuse than Sarah had, since no religious hope was in view; Calvin condemns both, Rachel for unlawful arts and Jacob for yielding to her, while conceding that the resulting union was afterwards honoured as marriage; Henry lays the blame further back, on the marriage to two sisters.
outliers: Henry's rabbinic saying that the keys of the clouds, the heart, the grave and the womb are trusted to neither angel nor seraph.
Ellicott's observation that Rachel says Elohim where Leah says Jehovah, and only uses the covenant name after bearing a child of her own.
Clarke's citation of an old English Bible which rendered the name Gad as the exclamation Good luck.
Calvin's concession that a connection void at its beginning nevertheless obtained, by special privilege, the honour of wedlock.

14.pericope_label: The mandrakes, and the last children born at Haran

schools.summary: Gill reports Bishop Patrick's explanation that the sisters' contest arose from their desire to fulfil the promise of a seed numerous as the stars and of the Messiah springing from it, which he takes to be why so much notice is given to matters otherwise below the dignity of sacred history. Calvin declines to identify the fruit, reads the episode as showing more than Moses states — a house filled with contention, the sisters permitted to quarrel so that the punishment of polygamy might be exhibited to posterity, and Jacob torn between parties because he had broken the unity of the conjugal bond — charges Leah with boasting of a son given as the reward of her sin while allowing that she was moved by a wish to increase her family rather than by lust, notes that genealogies commonly pass women over except where something worth commemorating befalls them and thinks Dinah probably the only daughter, and cautions that God is subject to no forgetfulness, Scripture speaking of his remembering from the effect produced upon us.

Henry will say only that the fruit was some rarity pleasant to the smell, perhaps jessamine, and turns aside to observe that God provides for our delights as well as our necessities, praising the custom of blessing him on tasting a pleasant fruit or smelling a flower; he makes Reuben a little lad of five or six, compares Leah's bargain with the advantage Jacob had taken of Esau's craving for the red pottage, and warns that there may be great sin and folly in an inordinate desire for a small thing, strong passions thwarting one another. He reports Bishop Patrick's account of the sisters' motive, and on the last name draws out its double sense, hesitating whether the hope of another son is inordinate desire or a faith that takes the present mercy as an earnest of more.

Clarke reports that learned men have wasted much labour guessing at the fruit, lists lilies, jessamine, citrons, mushrooms and figs among the proposals, and rests on Hasselquist, a pupil of Linnaeus, who found the mandrake ripe near Nazareth in early May, matching the wheat harvest; he adds that Greeks and Orientals held the plant to assist conception and that the Hebrew word means loves, thinks Rachel had by then engrossed her husband's whole company, and traces Rachel's son to the prayer her husband's rebuke had driven her to, so that faith obtained what impatience had prevented, reading the child's name as a prophecy answered in Benjamin. Wesley follows Henry on Reuben's age, on Bishop Patrick's explanation, and on the double sense of the last name.

Ellicott identifies the fruit confidently as the mandrake, describes the plant to its carrot-shaped root and single purple blossoms, and cites Tristram, who had often eaten it without any soporific effect, so that the name rests on superstition rather than property; from the intervals of the narrative he makes Reuben between fifteen and twenty rather than a small child, old enough to wander over the waste, and observes that mandrakes would not grow on tilled land. He answers Calvin by name over Leah's prayer, holding that since God is said to have hearkened to her she must have prayed, and that the objection has little weight against untrained country women whose one anxiety was offspring. On the sixth name he finds Leah unusually obscure, takes the first of her two words for the present a father adds beyond the marriage contract, can find no trace of the second, and canvasses two Syriac lexicographers and three versions before concluding that a woman's value rose with each son. He explains that Dinah is recorded for what her story cost Simeon and Levi, and that in the East a daughter's birth brings no feast. Keil and Delitzsch note that the second seven years ran out about the time of the last birth.

debates: How old Reuben was. Henry and Wesley make him a child of five or six at play; Ellicott reckons the intervals of the narrative and puts him between fifteen and twenty, arguing that only an older boy would be trusted to range over uncultivated country.

Whether Leah's prayer can have been genuine. Calvin holds that she boasts of a son given as the reward of her sin and proclaims merit instead of confessing a fault; Ellicott replies to him directly, arguing from the statement that God hearkened to her that she had prayed, and dismissing the objection as pressing too hard on untrained women.

What the fruit was. Clarke surveys the guesses and settles on the mandrake with Hasselquist's evidence from season and place; Ellicott identifies it confidently and adds Tristram's testimony against its supposed properties; Henry ventures only a fragrant rarity, perhaps jessamine; Calvin declines to adduce anything certain.
outliers: Henry's report of the custom of blessing God aloud on tasting a pleasant fruit or smelling a sweet flower.
Ellicott's citation of Tristram, who had eaten the fruit often and found in it no soporific or other effect at all.
Ellicott's appeal to two Syriac lexicographers, and to three ancient versions, for the sense of the sixth son's name.
Calvin's principle that Scripture speaks of God remembering from the effect produced upon us, since with him nothing is past or future.
themes: a husband hired for a night

25.pericope_label: Jacob asks leave to go, and the bargain over the flocks

schools.summary: Gill counts Jacob's whole stay at twenty years, fourteen for his wives and six for the cattle, repeats the Jewish observation that twelve children were born within seven of them while rejecting the further tale that each arrived with a twin, and reads the separation of the flocks as Laban's calculation that a flock of one colour would breed few exceptions, so that he should have Jacob's service for nothing. Calvin holds that Jacob's claim on Canaan rested on the divine grant rather than on birth, since a man whose father had lived unsettled could be laughed at for pleading native soil, and adds Laban's injustice and the hope of Esau's appeasement as lesser motives; on Laban's words he takes a middle way, that the blessing was as perceptible as if attested by prophecy, and infers from Laban's anxiety to keep him that Jacob had proved a horn of plenty. He finds the form of the compact clearest from the separation itself, notes that only cattle of one colour were left with Jacob and that this left him faint hope of gain, and therefore insists that Jacob acted on an oracle rather than on cunning, wishing to be enriched no other way than by God's will, while Laban caught greedily at what looked advantageous and was disappointed.

Henry admires Jacob for serving out even his second apprenticeship, holding that a good man does not change though he swear to his own hurt and that being deceived is no warrant for deceiving; he traces the request to go to Jacob's affection for Canaan as the land of promise, in which he could not think of settling short of it. Of Laban he says that churlish selfish men know how to give good words when it serves their ends, and that God often blesses bad men for the sake of their godly relations, though they seldom have either the wit to see it or the grace to own it. He notices Jacob's modesty in refusing to repeat Laban's own compliment, saying only that the Lord had blessed Laban since his coming, humble men taking more pleasure in doing good than in hearing of it.

Clarke glosses Laban's expression as to view attentively, to pry into, reads the phrase for Jacob's arrival as according to my footsteps, defines the words for the flock's markings from a root meaning to patch, and remarks that he had seen such flocks nowhere but in the islands of Shetland, whence he had brought specimens of Jacob's flock now feeding in Middlesex. He calls the difficulty of reconciling the terms with the separation extreme, rejects one common conjecture as unsatisfactory, and solves it by observing that nothing yet belonged to Jacob, so that Laban was removing not Jacob's property but everything Jacob might later claim, leaving him a flock without a single animal of the kind he was to be paid in. Wesley keeps to the plainer reading that Laban expected a flock of one colour to breed few exceptions and so to cost him nothing.

Ellicott stretches Jacob's whole stay to thirty-four years, arguing that he was too encumbered with young children to travel earlier and that Laban's fortune needed that long to grow; he renders Laban's verb I have divined, explains that it properly means to mutter a formula between the teeth, dismisses both the derivation from serpent-omens and the guess that Laban consulted his household gods, and concludes that the word had worn down to no more than I fancy, the reply being complimentary and inconclusive. He reads the phrase for Jacob's coming as at my foot and the increase as having broken forth with irresistible might, explains that eastern sheep are generally white and goats black or brown, distinguishes small speckles from large patches, doubts the rendering brown since the word usually means black and black sheep are rare in the East, and notes that striped coats occur in goats but never in sheep. He then breaks from the rest twice, correcting in time to come to to-morrow so as to make it a next-day audit at which any white sheep among the separated beasts would count as stolen, and arguing that the sons who received the flocks were Jacob's own, since Reuben was by then twenty-six; he reckons the three days' journey at thirty or forty miles. Keil and Delitzsch record the separation without comment.

debates: How long Jacob served Laban. Gill makes it twenty years in all, fourteen for the wives and six for the cattle; Ellicott stretches the stay to thirty-four, on the grounds that Jacob could not travel while his children were small and that Laban's wealth needed that long to accumulate.

Whose sons received the flocks that were separated. Gill, Wesley and Calvin all take them for Laban's; Ellicott argues they were Jacob's, since Reuben was twenty-six by this time and Jacob's interests would have suffered in Laban's hands, and adds that he could not have escaped six years later had his property been in their keeping.

What Laban means by saying he has learned by experience. Clarke glosses the verb as viewing attentively or prying into; Ellicott gives it the strong sense of muttering a magical formula while insisting the word had already faded to a mere I fancy; Calvin steers between, making the blessing as perceptible to Laban as if it had been attested by prophecy or found by augury.
outliers: Clarke's report that he had seen such flocks only in the islands of Shetland, and had brought specimens of Jacob's flock home to feed in Middlesex.
Ellicott's correction of in time to come to to-morrow, which turns the clause into a next-day inspection with a penalty for theft.
Henry's remark that God often blesses bad men for the sake of their godly relations, though they seldom have the wit to see it or the grace to own it.
Calvin's argument that Jacob's claim on Canaan rested on the divine grant and not on birth, since his father had lived there unsettled and always shifting his abode.
themes: a blessing owned by a churl

37.pericope_label: The peeled rods, and Jacob’s increase

schools.summary: Gill explains that the rods were cut fresh from the tree, that the feeble cattle were those already covered with wool and less fit for breeding, and that Jacob withheld the rods from them partly to keep his own flock sound and partly so as not to strip Laban of his whole stock; he adds that the surplus sheep were sold at a good price to buy camels and asses against a removal. Calvin refuses the defence that Jacob was merely repaying injury, since a man unjustly treated may not contend with equal injustice and private vengeance would leave no place for courts; he holds that Jacob ought to have overcome evil with good and would have been bound to, had heaven not commanded otherwise, and explains that the narrative puts last what came first, relating the act before the command behind it, so that those who meet fraud with fraud cannot claim Jacob as their advocate. To the objection that God cannot have prompted a deceit he answers that God is the author of no fraud when he stretches out a hand to protect his servant, and that no less should be conceded to him than to a human judge who sentences a thief to fourfold restitution; he also gives a physiological account of the device and notes that Jacob chose both his season and his place.

Henry sets out three contrivances — the peeled rods at the watering place, the parti-coloured beasts set where the rest must look at them, and the restriction of both to the stronger season — thinks the custom probably known to Canaanite shepherds, and draws from it that a man should be master of his trade, ingenious as well as industrious, since God teaches even the husbandman discretion; he remarks that strong impressions are made by the eye, with which we therefore need to make a covenant. He calls the policy honest, holding that its success would not justify it were there anything fraudulent in it, which he is sure there was not, since Jacob acted by divine direction, and concludes that those who are humble and industrious while their beginning is small are in a likely way to see their latter end increase.

Clarke takes the first tree for the white poplar, notes that the epithet means fresh rather than green since dry rods could not be peeled, leaves the second undecided between filbert and almond, and identifies the third as the plane, named from a root meaning naked because its bark sheds yearly, gathering Homer, Virgil and Petronius on the shade of that tree. He holds the belief about impressions on the mother long established and not yet rationally accounted for, yet within nature's powers, and doubts not the same trial would answer again; he explains the strong and feeble cattle as the early and late born and suggests English breeders would improve their stock by the same method. He closes by naming the chapter's four hard places and preferring to confess ignorance rather than multiply conjectures, allows that Laban's imposition of the elder daughter was foreign to every dictate of honesty, but calls Jacob's talent a dangerous one, traces the habit to his mother's teaching that a good end sanctifies any means, thinks he went beyond the divine warrant in spoiling Laban's breed, and takes the record's candour about its own hero for evidence of the historian's impartiality. Wesley repeats Henry's account almost word for word but stops short of his verdict, leaving the honesty of the device an open question.

Ellicott corrects all three trees from Tristram's field observation, making the first the storax, a perfumed shrub that whitens the hills of Galilee in March, the second the almond since the true hazel has never been found wild in Palestine, and the third the plane, the chestnut growing there only in Lebanese orchards; he explains that the vessels were the fixed troughs at the wells and that the notion of gutters feeding them is modern, calls the result of Jacob's device physically certain to follow, suggests that the parti-coloured young were massed together at watering so as to work on the flock's imagination, and makes wool the likelier source of Jacob's wealth, the camels marking the trade he was by then carrying on. Keil and Delitzsch record only that the feebler fell to Laban and the stronger to Jacob.

debates: What the three trees were. Clarke identifies poplar, an undecided filbert or almond, and plane; Ellicott revises the list to storax, almond and plane on Tristram's evidence that neither the wild hazel nor the chestnut grows in the country.

Whether the stratagem was honest. Henry pronounces it honest policy, resting on the divine direction; Wesley reproduces his account but withholds the verdict and defers the question; Calvin denies that the injuries received would excuse it and grounds the whole defence on the command alone; Clarke thinks Jacob exceeded even that warrant by ruining Laban's breed.

Whether the effect requires a miracle. Clarke holds it a natural if unexplained power and expects the same trial to succeed again; Ellicott calls the outcome physically certain; Calvin offers a physiological account; Henry ascribes the increase to a special blessing on the device.
outliers: Clarke's parade of Homer, Virgil and Petronius on the welcome shade of the plane tree.
Clarke's suggestion that breeders in his own country would improve their stock by adopting Jacob's method with the earlier-born cattle.
Clarke's tracing of Jacob's scheming habit to his mother's principle that a good end sanctifies any means, with his warning to parents against it.
Clarke's judgment that a record so unflattering to its own hero is itself evidence of the historian's impartiality.
themes: what the eye works on the womb
